A well-circumscribed, whorled gross appearance and submucosal location are classic; chronic abnormal uterine bleeding can cause microcytic iron-deficiency anemia. Histology shows bland, intersecting/whorled bundles of smooth-muscle cells. The source lists hemoglobin as 10.8 mg/dL, an apparent unit typo; the clinically appropriate unit is g/dL.

choice_explanations.A: Hyperchromatic glands invading myometrium indicate endometrial carcinoma, which is typically invasive and not a sharply demarcated whorled smooth-muscle mass.
choice_explanations.B: Endometrial glands within the myometrium describe adenomyosis, which usually causes diffuse, boggy uterine enlargement rather than a well-circumscribed tumor.
choice_explanations.C: Closely packed benign glands describe a hyperplastic endometrial polyp, not a whorled myometrial smooth-muscle tumor.
choice_explanations.D: Cystically dilated benign glands describe an atrophic endometrial polyp, not a leiomyoma.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Leiomyoma histology consists of well-demarcated whorled bundles of bland smooth-muscle cells.

A.text: Endometrial carcinoma is a separate uterine neoplasm; the well-demarcated whorled tumor instead matches myometrial leiomyoma.

B.text: Adenomyosis is endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, usually with diffuse boggy uterine enlargement.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe histology of hyperplastic endometrial polyps in this comparison.

D.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly describe cystically dilated endometrial polyp glands in this comparison.

E.text: Leiomyoma is a benign myometrial tumor with a gross whorled pattern of smooth-muscle bundles and well-demarcated borders.

stem: A 35-year-old woman sustains head trauma in a motor vehicle collision. She was an unrestrained passenger and hit her head on the windshield. Upon arrival in the emergency department, she is unresponsive. Respirations are 6/minute and pulse oximetry is 85% on facemask. Her pulse is 125/min and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. She is intubated for airway protection and admitted to the intensive care unit. One week later, her hemoglobin decreases from 12 g/dL to 9 g/dL. An upper endoscopy shows several gastric ulcers and diffuse gastritis. An increase in which of the following is the most likely explanation for her gastric lesions?
explanation: Severe physiologic stress after head trauma can produce acute stress-related gastric ulcers. Increased pepsin production can overwhelm weakened mucosal defenses; gastric acid production may also rise. Ulcers can still occur even without increased acid or pepsin when stress compromises those defenses. The First Aid association for CNS-injury (Cushing) ulcers emphasizes increased vagal stimulation, acetylcholine, and gastric H+ production.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. The stomach does not absorb acid in the way implied; acid is neutralized in the small intestine. Increased acid secretion, not absorption, may contribute to acute ulceration.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Bicarbonate neutralizes acid at the mucosal surface and is protective; increasing its transport would oppose injury.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretion and slows gastric emptying; it is not the cause of stress ulcers. CCK levels may fall in critically ill patients with reduced food intake.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Faster epithelial regeneration repairs mucosal defects and is protective against ulceration.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Gastric perfusion supports mucosal defenses. Stress-related ischemia/compromised blood flow promotes injury; increased flow would be protective.
choice_explanations.F: Incorrect. Mucus forms a protective barrier over the epithelium and limits exposure to acid and pepsin; increased secretion would be protective.
choice_explanations.G: Correct. In severe stress, pepsin production can overwhelm weakened gastric defenses and contribute to stress-ulcer formation.

A.text: No direct First Aid 2026 match for gastric acid absorption; the source explanation distinguishes absorption from acid production.

B.text: Bicarbonate from gastric and other mucosal cells neutralizes acid and is trapped in mucus covering the gastric epithelium; it is protective.

C.text: CCK is produced by duodenal/jejunal I cells and stimulates pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction; no direct ulcer-causing role is listed.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 entry was found for increased gastric epithelial regenerative capacity as a named ulcer mechanism; the protective interpretation follows the source explanation.

E.text: First Aid links burn-associated Curling ulcers to hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia, supporting impaired—not increased—mucosal perfusion as injurious.

F.text: No direct First Aid 2026 statement was found that increased mucus secretion prevents stress ulcers. The page 379 figure labels gastric mucus-related cells, but does not state the protective rationale in this choice.

G.text: Pepsin is produced by chief cells and digests protein; local acid and vagal stimulation increase secretion, and acid converts pepsinogen to active pepsin. Page 386 separately links brain injury to acute Cushing ulcers through increased vagal stimulation and gastric H+ production.

fa_summary: Acute gastritis/erosions can follow brain injury (Cushing ulcer) through increased vagal stimulation → increased ACh → increased gastric H+ production. First Aid also identifies pepsin as a chief-cell protein-digesting secretion increased by vagal stimulation/local acid, and bicarbonate as an acid-neutralizing mucosal defense.

stem: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of dark urine and grayish stools. Physical examination shows mild scleral icterus and right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies show a total bilirubin of 3.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 2.1 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase of 150 U/L, AST of 9 U/L, and ALT of 10 U/L. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Dark urine and pale/gray stools point to biliary obstruction. A common bile duct stone causes conjugated bilirubin to reflux into blood; water-soluble conjugated bilirubin is excreted in urine, darkening it, while reduced bilirubin delivery to the intestine lowers stercobilin and makes stools pale. The mild alkaline phosphatase elevation and normal AST/ALT support obstruction without substantial hepatocyte injury. Right upper quadrant tenderness with no severe pain is consistent with incomplete rather than total obstruction.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Hemolysis causes predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and may cause hemoglobinuria, but does not explain pale stools from absent intestinal bilirubin delivery.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. A common bile duct stone obstructs bile flow, producing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, dark urine, and pale stools.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Crigler-Najjar syndrome impairs bilirubin conjugation and causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, usually presenting early in life; it does not cause acholic stools.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Gilbert syndrome causes mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, often during fasting, illness, or stress, and does not cause dark urine with pale stools.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Viral hepatitis typically causes marked aminotransferase elevation and a mixed bilirubin pattern; it does not fit the near-normal AST/ALT or classic obstructive stool/urine findings.

A.text: Hemolysis is listed among causes of unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia, unlike this patient's predominant direct bilirubin.

B.text: Gallstones are a cause of biliary obstruction; page 400 classifies biliary tract obstruction as a cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

C.text: Crigler-Najjar syndrome is an inherited cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to absent or markedly reduced UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity.

D.text: Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, often with fasting, stress, or illness.

E.text: Hepatitis is listed as a cause of mixed hyperbilirubinemia, in contrast to the predominantly conjugated obstructive pattern here.

fa_summary: Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia suggests biliary obstruction or an excretion defect. Gallstones can obstruct the biliary tract; unconjugated bilirubin instead rises with hemolysis, Crigler-Najjar, or Gilbert syndrome. Hepatitis commonly produces mixed hyperbilirubinemia.

stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician for infertility evaluation. During the last 6 months she has had two positive pregnancy tests, but then menses began within days of the tests. She and her husband are healthy, with no known reproductive defects or chromosomal abnormalities. Which of the following laboratory findings in serum is most likely in this patient?
explanation: The positive pregnancy tests show that hCG was produced after implantation, but the very early loss of each pregnancy suggests inadequate support of the endometrium. In early pregnancy, hCG acts like LH to maintain the corpus luteum, which supplies progesterone until the placental shift. Failure to maintain the corpus luteum lowers progesterone, causing endometrial breakdown and pregnancy loss.

choice_explanations.A: High estrogen is not the expected defect causing repeated very early pregnancy loss; estrogen normally rises during pregnancy.
choice_explanations.B: hCG is present because the pregnancy tests are positive; hCG normally supports the corpus luteum rather than causing its failure.
choice_explanations.C: hPL is produced by syncytiotrophoblast and rises with placental mass; it is not the hormone maintaining the corpus luteum at this stage.
choice_explanations.D: Progesterone should be adequate to maintain the endometrium; low rather than high progesterone explains the losses.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Inadequate progesterone support after corpus-luteum regression leads to endometrial atrophy and early pregnancy loss.

A.text: Placental estrogen rises during pregnancy, but the First Aid discussion does not identify elevated estrogen as a cause of this pattern of early loss.

B.text: Syncytiotrophoblast-derived hCG maintains the corpus luteum in the first trimester; the pregnancy test detects hCG.

C.text: hPL is a placental hormone that rises with placental mass; it is distinct from hCG-mediated corpus-luteum support.

D.text: Progesterone is mainly secreted by the corpus luteum during the first 10 weeks and maintains the endometrium.

E.text: hCG maintains the corpus luteum, increasing first-trimester progesterone; progesterone maintains the endometrium.

stem: A 27-year-old primigravid woman at 39 weeks' gestation is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. Another car struck the side of the car where she was a passenger. She was wearing her seat belt. She reports abdominal pain and has premature rupture of the amniotic membranes and contractions. Ultrasound reveals fetal tachycardia and placental abruption. Which of the following is she most likely to experience as a result of amniotic fluid entering the circulation?
explanation: This is amniotic fluid embolism, a rare obstetric emergency associated with events such as placental abruption, uterine trauma, and delivery. Amniotic contents entering maternal veins lodge in the pulmonary microcirculation and trigger cardiopulmonary and inflammatory effects, causing abrupt respiratory distress; disseminated intravascular coagulation may follow. The source explanation identifies respiratory distress as the immediate expected manifestation.

choice_explanations.A: Hemiplegia is a focal neurologic deficit and is not the characteristic immediate presentation of amniotic fluid embolism.
choice_explanations.B: Preeclampsia is a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy, not the acute pulmonary manifestation of amniotic fluid entering maternal circulation.
choice_explanations.C: Proteinuria can accompany preeclampsia but is not the immediate consequence tested here.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden respiratory distress from pulmonary microvascular obstruction and mediator effects; coagulopathy may also occur.
choice_explanations.E: Splinter hemorrhages are classically associated with infective endocarditis, not amniotic fluid embolism.

A.text: No direct First Aid 2026 reproductive-page discussion links hemiplegia to amniotic fluid embolism.

B.text: First Aid discusses preeclampsia separately, but not as a consequence of amniotic fluid embolism.

C.text: Proteinuria is discussed with preeclampsia, not as the acute manifestation of amniotic fluid embolism.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 reproductive-page entry for amniotic fluid embolism or its acute respiratory presentation was found; this mapping is supported by the source explanation.

E.text: No direct First Aid 2026 reproductive-page mapping connects splinter hemorrhages with this obstetric emergency.

stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fever, chills, body aches, painful urination, and urinary urgency. His medical history includes well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes managed with oral hypoglycemic agents. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 134/88 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, hematocrit 40%, and leukocyte count 12,800/mm³. Physical examination shows mild abdominal tenderness. Digital rectal examination shows a diffusely enlarged, very tender prostate gland. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
explanation: Fever, dysuria, urgency, leukocytosis, and a warm, enlarged, markedly tender prostate indicate acute bacterial prostatitis. In older men, Escherichia coli is the most common cause. Other gram-negative organisms can cause prostatitis, but they are less likely than E. coli in this presentation.

choice_explanations.A: Enterobacter can cause urinary infection but is not the most common cause of acute bacterial prostatitis in older men.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. E. coli is the most common cause of acute bacterial prostatitis in older men.
choice_explanations.C: Klebsiella is a possible urinary pathogen but is less common than E. coli in this setting.
choice_explanations.D: Proteus can cause urinary infection, particularly with urease-related stones, but is not the most likely organism here.
choice_explanations.E: Pseudomonas is a possible pathogen in selected healthcare-associated or instrumented urinary infections, but not the most common cause in this case.

A.text: First Aid lists Enterobacter among less-common acute bacterial prostatitis pathogens in older males; E. coli is most common.

B.text: Acute bacterial prostatitis in older males is most commonly caused by E. coli.

C.text: Klebsiella is included among other possible bacterial pathogens; E. coli remains the most common cause in older males.

D.text: Proteus is included among other possible bacterial pathogens; E. coli remains the most common cause in older males.

E.text: Pseudomonas is included among other possible bacterial pathogens; E. coli remains the most common cause in older males.

stem: A 29-year-old man who is a construction worker is brought to the emergency department because of severe penetrating wounds to the abdomen. An emergent exploratory laparotomy is performed and the wounds are sutured. Before the abdominal cavity is closed, a small but well-formed uterus is found. Which of the following abnormalities during fetal development best explains the presence of a uterus in this otherwise normal male?
explanation: Sertoli cells in a developing testis produce Müllerian-inhibiting substance (MIS, also called anti-Müllerian hormone), which suppresses the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts. Deficiency of this signal allows female internal structures, including a uterus, to persist despite otherwise male development. Testosterone supports Wolffian structures, and dihydrotestosterone supports male external genital development; defects in those pathways do not by themselves explain a uterus in an otherwise normally virilized male.

choice_explanations.A: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency impairs conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone and affects male external genital development; it does not cause persistence of a uterus.
choice_explanations.B: Absence of testis-determining factor prevents normal testis development, so this does not fit an otherwise normally developed male with a specific persistent Müllerian structure.
choice_explanations.C: An LH-secreting tumor could alter androgen production but would not remove the fetal Sertoli-cell signal that suppresses Müllerian ducts.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Without Müllerian-inhibiting substance from Sertoli cells, Müllerian ducts persist and form a uterus despite male internal/external structures.
choice_explanations.E: Testosterone deficiency disrupts Wolffian duct development and male differentiation; it does not specifically explain persistence of the Müllerian-derived uterus in an otherwise normal male.

A.text: 5α-reductase deficiency prevents conversion of testosterone to DHT and affects male external genital differentiation, not Müllerian duct regression.

B.text: Testis-determining factor from the SRY gene drives testis development; Sertoli-cell MIS then suppresses Müllerian ducts.

C.text: First Aid 2026 does not directly discuss an LH-secreting tumor as a cause of persistent Müllerian structures.

D.text: Absence of Müllerian-inhibiting substance permits both male and female internal genitalia to develop in an XY individual.

E.text: Testosterone supports Wolffian duct development; DHT supports male external genital differentiation. Neither is the Müllerian-suppressing signal.

stem: A 79-year-old man comes to the physician because of difficulty swallowing and a feeling of a lump in his throat. He has not noticed any changes in his weight. He occasionally regurgitates undigested food shortly after eating. He has noticed foul odor from his breath and occasional changes in his voice. A frame from a videofluoroscopic study of a barium swallow is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is Zenker diverticulum, a false pharyngoesophageal diverticulum caused by mucosa and submucosa herniating through a weak area near the pharynx–esophagus junction (Killian triangle). Retained food can cause regurgitation of undigested material and halitosis; dysphagia, globus sensation, and voice change also fit. The barium study shows an outpouching that retains contrast above the cricopharyngeus. Routine endoscopy and nasogastric-tube placement are avoided because of perforation risk.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Achalasia is a motility disorder with impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis; barium swallow shows distal narrowing with proximal esophageal dilation rather than a pharyngoesophageal pouch.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Esophageal cancer typically causes progressive dysphagia and weight loss. The retained-contrast outpouching and absence of weight loss favor Zenker diverticulum.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Mallory-Weiss tears are longitudinal mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful vomiting, usually presenting with hematemesis.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. A Schatzki ring is a distal mucosal ring near the squamocolumnar junction and may cause intermittent food sticking; it does not cause a pharyngoesophageal pouch, halitosis, or voice change.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. A traction diverticulum is a true diverticulum involving all esophageal wall layers, usually caused by adherence to a scarred mediastinal structure; it is distinct from the false pharyngoesophageal pouch shown here.
choice_explanations.F: Correct. Zenker diverticulum produces an upper esophageal pouch that traps food, causing dysphagia, regurgitation, halitosis, and sometimes voice change.

A.text: Achalasia is an esophageal motility disorder with impaired LES relaxation, absent peristalsis, and a dilated esophagus with bird's-beak narrowing on barium swallow.

B.text: Esophageal cancer typically presents with progressive dysphagia and weight loss and has an aggressive course.

C.text: Mallory-Weiss syndrome is a partial-thickness longitudinal tear at the gastroesophageal junction due to repeated vomiting.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 entry for Schatzki ring was found.

E.text: No direct First Aid 2026 entry for traction esophageal diverticulum was found.

F.text: Zenker diverticulum is a pharyngoesophageal false diverticulum caused by mucosal/submucosal herniation at Killian triangle; symptoms include dysphagia, obstruction, gurgling, aspiration, foul breath, and neck mass, especially in older men.

fa_summary: Zenker diverticulum is a false pharyngoesophageal pouch at Killian triangle. In older adults it causes dysphagia, regurgitation/retention, halitosis, and sometimes voice change; diagnose with barium swallow. Avoid routine endoscopy or NG tubes because of perforation risk.
question_figure_description: Only the relevant lateral videofluoroscopic barium-study image is retained; question text, answer choices, answer markings, and interface are excluded.

stem: A 49-year-old woman comes to the physician because she noticed a lump in her breast during self-examination. A biopsy specimen shows invasive ductal carcinoma. The connective tissue adjacent to the nests of tumor is very densely collagenous. Which of the following best describes this type of pathologic change in the connective tissue?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This is an example of desmoplasia, which is excessive fibrous tissue formation in the stroma surrounding the tumor. The abundant fibrous tissue growth itself is benign and simply a reaction to tumor invasion of healthy tissue. Desmoplasia is usually seen with malignant neoplasms, although benign processes such as surgical scars can also constitute a desmoplastic reaction. Ultimately, desmoplasia is initiated by injury to healthy tissue, whether through malignancy or physical injury. Injury triggers growth-factor production, fibroblast proliferation, and increased extracellular matrix. In certain cancers, including pancreatic cancer, desmoplasia is thought to induce chemoresistance because of poor permeability of chemotherapeutic agents through the dense fibrosis. Another reaction to tumor invasion is a lymphocytic response, such as that seen in testicular seminoma and medullary carcinoma of the breast.

Anaplasia (choice A) is a term for tumors that show severe loss of cell differentiation and tissue organization. These cells tend to be large (“big and ugly”). Anaplastic tumors are typically much more clinically aggressive than their well-differentiated counterparts. An example is anaplastic thyroid cancer.

Carcinoma in situ (choice B) also demonstrates severe cellular dysplasia; however, these changes are extensive enough to be classified as cancer. Unlike invasive carcinoma, the changes are confined to the epithelium, involve its full thickness, do not penetrate the underlying basement membrane, and do not invade underlying tissue.

Dysplasia (choice D) is atypical cellular proliferation. Examples include colonic tubular adenomas, HPV-infected cervical lesions, and actinic keratosis of the skin. Dysplasia is a precursor to cancer, although not all dysplasia progresses because some dysplasias can regress. Dysplastic changes include increased cell size, an increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, abnormal shape (poikilocytosis), nuclear hyperpigmentation, loss of cellular architectural organization (loss of apical-versus-basal orientation), and mitotic figures.

Metaplasia (choice E) is replacement of one type of differentiated cell or tissue by another type not normally present at that site. In smokers, normal ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium of the respiratory tract is replaced with stratified squamous epithelium. In patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), normal stratified squamous epithelium of the esophagus is replaced by glandular columnar epithelium. In both cases, metaplastic changes may progress to dysplasia and ultimately carcinoma (squamous cell carcinoma of the lung in smokers and esophageal adenocarcinoma in patients with GERD).

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Anaplasia describes marked loss of differentiation and tissue organization in tumor cells; it does not describe collagen-rich supporting stroma.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Carcinoma in situ is severe epithelial dysplasia that has not penetrated the basement membrane. This biopsy already shows invasive carcinoma and the question asks about its surrounding connective tissue.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. Desmoplasia is excessive fibrous tissue formation in tumor stroma, often as a reaction to invasion of adjacent healthy tissue.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Dysplasia is disordered atypical cellular growth, not a collagenous stromal reaction.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Metaplasia is replacement of one differentiated cell type by another in response to stress; it is not fibrosis around a tumor.

A.text: First Aid describes anaplastic tumors as undifferentiated, high-grade malignant tumors; this is a tumor-cell differentiation concept rather than a stromal response.

B.text: Carcinoma in situ is severe dysplasia through the full epithelial thickness without basement-membrane penetration.

C.text: First Aid discusses supporting connective-tissue stroma and invasive carcinoma on p.215, but does not directly name or define desmoplasia; use the source explanation for this term.

D.text: Dysplasia is loss of uniformity in cell size and shape, tissue orientation, and normal nuclear features.

E.text: Metaplasia is reprogramming of stem cells with replacement of one differentiated cell type by another.

fa_summary: First Aid 2026 printed p.215 describes neoplasms as having neoplastic parenchyma and supporting stroma, and distinguishes dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, and invasive carcinoma. Printed p.216 uses anaplastic to describe an undifferentiated high-grade tumor. Printed p.202 defines metaplasia as replacement of one differentiated cell type by another. First Aid does not name or define desmoplasia specifically; the source explanation supplies that definition and relates it to tumor-associated fibrous stromal reaction.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents after they observe him ingest a small plastic toy building block. His parents are reassured that the block will most likely be eliminated during normal bowel movements and, if not, will be propelled through the gastrointestinal tract by periodic sequential contractions that begin in the stomach and gradually migrate to the ileum during fasting. Release of which of the following intestinal hormones is most likely responsible for this periodic event?
explanation: Motilin is released by the small intestine during fasting. Its cyclical release triggers migrating motor complexes (MMCs), peristaltic waves that begin in the stomach and travel to the ileum every 90–120 minutes. MMCs have a cleansing function, clearing residual material between meals; eating interrupts this activity.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. CCK is released from duodenal/jejunal I cells in response to fat and protein digestion products; it stimulates pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction during digestion, not fasting MMCs.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Gastrin is released from antral G cells, mainly during the gastric digestive phase; it increases acid secretion and motility but does not trigger fasting MMCs.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Gastrin-releasing peptide is a vagal neuropeptide that stimulates G cells to release gastrin; it is not the hormone that initiates MMCs.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. Small-intestinal motilin is released during fasting and causes migrating motor complexes.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Secretin is released from duodenal S cells in response to acid and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion; it is not a fasting motility hormone.
choice_explanations.F: Incorrect. Somatostatin from gastric/duodenal D cells inhibits gastrin secretion and is not the hormone responsible for MMCs.

A.text: CCK is released by I cells in the duodenum/jejunum and stimulates pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction.

B.text: Gastrin is released by G cells in the antrum/duodenum and increases gastric H+ secretion and motility.

C.text: First Aid describes vagal stimulation of gastrin release via gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP).

D.text: Motilin from the small intestine produces migrating motor complexes and is increased in the fasting state.

E.text: Secretin is released from duodenal S cells in response to acid and increases pancreatic bicarbonate secretion while decreasing gastric acid secretion.

F.text: Somatostatin from D cells in the pancreatic islets/GI mucosa suppresses gastric acid and pepsinogen secretion and inhibits release of several hormones.

fa_summary: Motilin is secreted by the small intestine during fasting and produces migrating motor complexes, periodic cleansing contractions that move from stomach toward ileum. Eating interrupts MMC activity.

stem: A 76-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 6-hour history of bloody diarrhea. She has had diffuse crampy abdominal pain for the past 3 days and has experienced similar episodes before, although they usually do not last long. Her history includes stable angina, hypercholesterolemia, myocardial infarction 10 years ago, and cerebral infarction 3 years ago with good recovery. She denies recent travel. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 100/66 mm Hg. Examination shows vague left upper quadrant abdominal tenderness without a palpable mass. Rectal examination reveals no mass or hemorrhoids, but bright red blood is present on the glove. Colonoscopy shows patchy mucosal ulcerations near the splenic flexure. Which of the following most likely contributed to her presentation?
explanation:
The correct answer is A. Ischemic bowel disease is seen particularly in patients older than 70 years, has a female-predominant distribution, and presents with crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. It involves watershed zones: (1) the splenic flexure, supplied by the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, and (2) the sigmoid colon, supplied by the inferior mesenteric, pudendal, and iliac arteries. Hypoperfusion or occlusion of these vessels (thrombus, embolism, or stenosis) causes focal ischemic colitis. This patient’s history of hypercholesterolemia and cardiovascular ischemia suggests atherosclerosis of the affected vessels.

Gluten sensitivity (choice B) is associated with celiac disease. It affects the second part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the colon. Patients may also have dermatitis herpetiformis. Endoscopically, there may be mucosal erythema and atrophy. It can occur in children and adults; villous atrophy leads to malabsorption and weight loss, and histology shows villous atrophy and lymphocytic infiltrate.

Protozoal infection (choice C) may indicate amoebic dysentery, which can result from ingestion of infective cysts in contaminated water or food. Patients may be asymptomatic or have abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. However, diffuse colonic involvement would be expected rather than disease limited to the splenic flexure. Colonoscopy may reveal small ulcers; histology shows flask-shaped ulcers and acute inflammation. Liver abscesses may also occur. The patient denies travel, and the focal location does not fit amoebic dysentery.

Structural weakening (choice D) suggests diverticulosis, acquired outpouchings of colonic mucosa. It commonly affects adults older than 50 years and the left side of the colon (sigmoid, rather than the splenic flexure) in Western countries; right-sided involvement is more common in Asia and Africa. Clinically, there can be alternating constipation and diarrhea and episodic crampy abdominal pain. Impaction of a fecalith may cause diverticulitis with pain, bleeding, and potential rupture. A high-fiber diet can help reduce stool bulk.

Vascular malformation (choice E) suggests angiodysplasia: dilated, malformed submucosal and mucosal vessels prone to rupture and significant bleeding. It can present as acute or intermittent bleeding and commonly occurs in the cecum or right colon in patients older than 60 years. Although uncommon, it accounts for approximately 20% of lower intestinal hemorrhage and can be associated with Osler-Weber-Rendu and CREST syndrome. This patient has mucosal ulcerations rather than prominent mucosal vessels, and the location does not correspond to angiodysplasia.

ReKaps: Ischemic colitis is usually due to atherosclerosis, other forms of occlusion, or hypoperfusion. It is seen in older patients, more often women, and presents with intermittent cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. The splenic flexure and sigmoid colon are common sites because they are watershed zones.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. Atherosclerosis can narrow mesenteric vessels and cause focal ischemia at watershed regions such as the splenic flexure, producing crampy pain and bloody diarrhea.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Gluten-sensitive enteropathy primarily affects the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum, causing malabsorption/steatorrhea rather than focal colonic watershed ulcers and hematochezia.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. Entamoeba histolytica can cause bloody diarrhea and flask-shaped ulcers, but typically causes infectious colitis with broader involvement; no travel history and the watershed distribution plus vascular history favor ischemia.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Structural weakening suggests colonic diverticulosis, usually involving the sigmoid colon; diverticular bleeding is typically painless, and diverticulitis generally causes focal LLQ pain rather than splenic-flexure ischemic ulcers.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. Angiodysplasia causes bleeding from dilated mucosal/submucosal vessels, commonly in the right colon of older adults, rather than patchy ulcers at the splenic-flexure watershed.

A.text: Colonic ischemia causes crampy pain followed by hematochezia at watershed sites including the splenic flexure; older adults are typically affected. First Aid also describes chronic mesenteric ischemia from atherosclerosis of the celiac artery/SMA/IMA.

B.text: Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) primarily affects distal duodenum/proximal jejunum and causes malabsorption/steatorrhea.

C.text: Entamoeba histolytica causes amebiasis with bloody diarrhea/dysentery and flask-shaped colonic ulcers; this infection is a distractor to the watershed pattern.

D.text: Colonic diverticulosis consists of false diverticula at focal weak points, commonly in the sigmoid; diverticular bleeding can cause painless hematochezia.

E.text: Angiodysplasia consists of tortuous dilated vessels that cause hematochezia, most often in the right colon and in older patients.

fa_summary: Colonic ischemia presents with crampy abdominal pain followed by hematochezia and commonly affects watershed regions, especially the splenic flexure, in older adults. Atherosclerotic mesenteric disease can reduce perfusion. Distinguish from celiac malabsorption, amebic dysentery, sigmoid diverticulosis, and right-sided angiodysplasia.

stem: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommate because of abdominal pain and vomiting. He took an entire bottle of acetaminophen tablets that morning in a suicide attempt. His vital signs and temperature are within normal limits. There is right upper quadrant tenderness. Which of the following sets of serum laboratory findings is most likely in this patient?

options.text: AST high; ALT high; alkaline phosphatase high; amylase normal
AST high; ALT high; alkaline phosphatase normal; amylase normal
AST high; ALT low; alkaline phosphatase high; amylase high
AST normal; ALT normal; alkaline phosphatase high; amylase normal
AST normal; ALT high; alkaline phosphatase normal; amylase high

explanation: Acetaminophen overdose causes hepatocellular injury through the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which can produce massive hepatic necrosis. Injured hepatocytes release AST and ALT, often into the thousands, while alkaline phosphatase (primarily associated with bile ducts) and amylase (used in pancreatitis) are not expected to rise from isolated acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis. The laboratory-pattern table is transcribed into each option below rather than reproducing the whole screenshot.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. Concurrent elevation of AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase suggests a mixed/severe hepatobiliary pattern; acetaminophen toxicity classically causes marked aminotransferase elevation without a corresponding alkaline phosphatase or amylase elevation.
choice_explanations.B: Correct. Acute hepatocellular necrosis causes high AST and ALT, while alkaline phosphatase and amylase are usually normal.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. This pattern is not the expected hepatocellular injury pattern; low ALT with high alkaline phosphatase and amylase does not fit acetaminophen toxicity.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation suggests cholestasis, infiltrative liver disease, or bone disease rather than hepatocyte necrosis.
choice_explanations.E: Incorrect. High amylase suggests pancreatic injury, and normal AST with high ALT is not the usual marked aminotransferase pattern in acetaminophen-induced hepatic necrosis.

A.text: First Aid describes alkaline phosphatase elevation in cholestasis/infiltrative disease and marked aminotransferase elevations in acute liver injury; the combined ALP rise is not the typical isolated acetaminophen pattern.

B.text: AST and ALT rise in most liver disease and can rise markedly in drug-induced liver injury such as acetaminophen toxicity; alkaline phosphatase is associated with cholestasis, while amylase is not a liver marker.

C.text: No direct First Aid 2026 pattern matching high AST, low ALT, and simultaneous high alkaline phosphatase/amylase was found; the pattern does not match acetaminophen hepatocellular injury.

D.text: Alkaline phosphatase is elevated in cholestasis, infiltrative disorders, and bone disease; isolated elevation is not the expected finding in acute acetaminophen hepatocellular injury.

E.text: First Aid identifies ALT/AST as liver-injury markers; isolated amylase elevation is not a marker of acetaminophen hepatic necrosis.

fa_summary: Acetaminophen overdose can cause acute hepatic necrosis with very high AST/ALT. First Aid distinguishes hepatocellular enzyme release from alkaline phosphatase elevations in cholestasis; N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione as the specific antidote.

stem: A 20-year-old woman with a history of sickle cell disease is referred to a surgeon because of biliary colic. She undergoes cholecystectomy, and black pigment stones are seen in her gallbladder on gross examination. The graph shows gallstone composition by cholesterol (vertical axis) and unconjugated bilirubin (horizontal axis). Which point most likely represents the composition of this patient's gallstones?
explanation: Sickle cell disease causes chronic hemolysis and increased heme turnover, increasing unconjugated bilirubin in bile. Unconjugated bilirubin is insoluble and can precipitate with calcium as calcium bilirubinate, forming black pigment stones. These stones therefore have high unconjugated bilirubin and relatively low/normal cholesterol, corresponding to point E on the graph.

choice_explanations.A: Incorrect. High cholesterol with low unconjugated bilirubin is the cholesterol-stone pattern, not black pigment stones associated with chronic hemolysis.
choice_explanations.B: Incorrect. Low levels of both plotted components do not match calcium bilirubinate stones produced by excess unconjugated bilirubin.
choice_explanations.C: Incorrect. An intermediate/mixed composition is not the expected black pigment-stone pattern in chronic hemolysis.
choice_explanations.D: Incorrect. High cholesterol and high unconjugated bilirubin suggests a mixed composition; black pigment stones are high in unconjugated bilirubin but low or normal in cholesterol.
choice_explanations.E: Correct. Black pigment stones contain calcium bilirubinate and are associated with hemolysis, so unconjugated bilirubin is high while cholesterol is low/normal.

A.text: Cholesterol stones are the cholesterol-rich stone type; First Aid lists obesity, estrogen, multiparity, rapid weight loss, and other risk factors.

B.text: No direct First Aid 2026 category for low cholesterol and low unconjugated bilirubin as a gallstone-composition pattern was found.

C.text: No direct First Aid 2026 description of the mixed/intermediate gallstone-composition point was found; the distractor is explained from the verified source graph and explanation.

D.text: No direct First Aid 2026 description of this high-cholesterol/high-bilirubin mixed composition was found; the distractor is explained from the verified source graph and explanation.

E.text: Pigment stones (black) are calcium bilirubinate and are associated with chronic hemolysis; the figure links hemolysis to increased unconjugated bilirubin and pigment-stone formation.

fa_summary: Chronic hemolysis increases bilirubin load and favors black pigment stones composed of calcium bilirubinate. On a cholesterol-versus-unconjugated-bilirubin graph, this is low/normal cholesterol and high unconjugated bilirubin (point E).
question_figure_description: Only the relevant gallstone-composition graph with axes and labeled points A–E is included; the screenshot interface, question and explanation are excluded.

stem: A 21-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of the abrupt onset of left-sided abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.7°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show elevated hCG levels. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an empty uterus and a gestational sac containing a yolk sac in the patient's left fallopian tube. Which of the following is the most likely predisposing factor for this condition?
explanation: The extrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac confirms a tubal ectopic pregnancy. Pelvic inflammatory disease can cause salpingitis, tubal scarring, and adhesions that delay passage of the fertilized ovum, increasing the risk of tubal implantation. Endometriosis, an IUD, leiomyomas, and prior surgery can also be associated with ectopic pregnancy, but PID-related tubal scarring is the strongest choice here.

choice_explanations.A: Endometriosis can cause peritubal adhesions, but it is a less likely predisposing factor than PID in this presentation.
choice_explanations.B: An IUD lowers the absolute incidence of pregnancy; if pregnancy occurs with an IUD, ectopic pregnancy is relatively more likely, but PID is the stronger risk factor here.
choice_explanations.C: Leiomyomas can distort the uterus and interfere with implantation, but are less likely than PID-related tubal scarring.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. PID can scar the fallopian tubes and impair transport of the fertilized ovum, predisposing to tubal ectopic pregnancy.
choice_explanations.E: Prior pelvic surgery can produce adhesions and raise ectopic risk, but PID is the most likely factor among these choices.

A.text: Endometriosis is described as ectopic endometrial tissue and can cause infertility; the ectopic-pregnancy entry specifically emphasizes tubal pathology as the risk pathway.

B.text: An IUD is listed as an ectopic-pregnancy risk factor, although it reduces pregnancy overall.

C.text: First Aid describes leiomyoma as a uterine smooth-muscle tumor but does not directly identify it as an ectopic-pregnancy risk factor.

D.text: Tubal scarring from salpingitis/PID is a listed risk factor for ectopic pregnancy.

E.text: Prior tubal/pelvic surgery is listed among ectopic-pregnancy risk factors.

stem: Fifty pregnant women participate in a study during which hormone levels are measured at different gestational times. Which of the following hormone profiles shown in the graph will most likely be seen in a woman with a normal pregnancy? W, X, and Y label the three curves; the table gives the candidate hormone assignments.

options.text: W: hCG; X: human placental lactogen (hPL); Y: corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)
W: progesterone; X: CRH; Y: hCG

explanation: The early-peaking curve W is hCG: it rises soon after implantation, peaks in the first trimester, and then declines. Curve X rises with placental mass throughout pregnancy, matching hPL. Curve Y rises sharply late in gestation, matching placental CRH. Thus the correct assignment is hCG, hPL, and CRH, respectively.

choice_explanations.A: Correct. hCG peaks early and then falls; hPL rises with placental mass; placental CRH rises sharply late in pregnancy.
choice_explanations.B: Progesterone does not follow the early sharp peak shown by W, and hCG is not the late-rising curve Y.
choice_explanations.C: The hCG and progesterone assignments do not match the steadily rising X curve and late-rising Y curve.
choice_explanations.D: hPL rises with placental mass rather than peaking early as W does; 17-hydroxyprogesterone does not match the late CRH-like Y curve.
choice_explanations.E: W is correctly assigned as hCG, but X matches rising hPL rather than 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and Y is the late-rising CRH curve rather than progesterone.

A.text: First Aid describes hCG peaking in early pregnancy and hPL rising with placental mass; the complete three-curve assignment is visually verified against the source figure.

B.text: The hCG profile is the early peak and decline, not the curve that rises sharply late in gestation.

C.text: The hCG and progesterone descriptions on the placental-hormone page do not support these curve assignments.

D.text: hPL rises with placental mass, unlike the early-peaking W curve; hCG is not the late-rising curve.

E.text: First Aid 2026 reproductive pages do not directly present a 17-hydroxyprogesterone gestational curve for this comparison; the source figure identifies X as the steadily increasing hPL curve and Y as late-rising CRH.

fa_subchapter: Adrenal steroids and congenital adrenal hyperplasias
stem: A newborn 46,XX girl shows signs of virilization. Her blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg and her serum potassium is 3.2 mEq/L. Laboratory studies show elevated plasma androgens and 17-hydroxyprogesterone and decreased aldosterone. A diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia is made. Which enzyme is most likely defective?
explanation: Virilization and androgen excess indicate diversion of steroid precursors into androgen synthesis. Hypertension and hypokalemia indicate mineralocorticoid activity from elevated 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC), while low aldosterone reflects renin-angiotensin suppression. 11β-hydroxylase deficiency blocks conversion of DOC to corticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol, causing DOC accumulation and this characteristic pattern.

choice_explanations.A: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes androgen excess and salt wasting with hypotension/hyperkalemia, not DOC-mediated hypertension and hypokalemia.
choice_explanations.B: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency causes impaired mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid synthesis with salt wasting; it does not cause DOC accumulation with hypertension.
choice_explanations.C: Correct. 11β-hydroxylase deficiency causes increased DOC, hypertension, hypokalemia, and androgen excess with virilization.
choice_explanations.D: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency reduces androgen production and causes hypertension/hypokalemia; virilization and elevated androgens argue against it.
choice_explanations.E: Aldosterone synthase deficiency lowers aldosterone but does not explain androgen excess, elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and DOC-mediated hypertension.

A.text: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes virilization but typically salt wasting, hypotension, and hyperkalemia; the CAH comparison table distinguishes it from 11β-hydroxylase deficiency.

B.text: First Aid 2026 does not include 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase as a separate row in its CAH comparison table; it does identify the major 17α-, 21-, and 11β-hydroxylase patterns.

C.text: The CAH table links 11β-hydroxylase deficiency to increased blood pressure, decreased potassium, and virilization in XX individuals.

D.text: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency causes hypertension but reduces sex-hormone production and does not cause virilization.

E.text: First Aid 2026 does not separately map aldosterone synthase deficiency in the CAH comparison table; this option cannot explain the androgen excess and hypertension pattern.

stem: A sexually active 25-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine gynecologic examination. Pelvic examination shows an area of abnormal-appearing epithelium on the cervix. Microscopic examination of a biopsy specimen shows nuclear enlargement and perinuclear vacuolization in the cervical epithelium. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?

options.text: Infection with human papillomavirus serotypes 6 and 11

explanation: Nuclear enlargement with perinuclear vacuolization (a perinuclear halo) and raisinoid, irregular nuclei are koilocytotic changes caused by HPV infection. Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 are associated with condyloma/koilocytosis. High-risk types 16 and 18 are associated with severe dysplasia and cervical carcinoma, which are not the described cytopathic changes.

choice_explanations.A: Gonorrhea causes mucopurulent cervicitis and neutrophilic inflammation, not koilocytosis.
choice_explanations.B: HSV can cause multinucleation and intranuclear inclusions or ground-glass nuclei, rather than the perinuclear halos of koilocytes.
choice_explanations.C: Chlamydia can cause cervicitis and intracytoplasmic inclusions, but not HPV-type koilocytosis.
choice_explanations.D: Correct. HPV infection produces koilocytes with irregular, raisinoid nuclei and perinuclear halos; types 6 and 11 are low-risk types associated with condyloma.
choice_explanations.E: Severe squamous dysplasia is associated with high-risk HPV, especially types 16 and 18, and is not identified by isolated koilocytosis.
choice_explanations.F: Squamous carcinoma in situ is associated with high-risk HPV and neoplastic epithelial changes, not the characteristic benign koilocytotic pattern alone.
choice_explanations.G: Trichomoniasis causes vaginitis with motile organisms and inflammation; it does not cause koilocytosis.

A.text: Gonorrhea is listed as an STI caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae; it does not produce the koilocytes described here.

B.text: Genital herpes is listed with vesicles/ulcers; the cervical koilocyte finding instead indicates HPV.

C.text: Chlamydia trachomatis D–K causes cervicitis/PID; it is distinct from HPV-related koilocytosis.

D.text: First Aid identifies koilocytes with condylomata acuminata and HPV-6/-11; the cervical pathology section describes koilocytes as pathognomonic of HPV infection.

E.text: High-risk HPV types 16 and 18 are associated with severe dysplasia and cervical cancer, not the low-risk HPV koilocytosis pattern.

F.text: The cervical pathology section notes progression to carcinoma in situ/invasive disease with high-risk HPV, distinct from the initial koilocytotic finding.

G.text: Trichomoniasis is listed as vaginitis due to Trichomonas vaginalis, with strawberry cervix/motile organisms rather than koilocytosis.
