A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a puffy face and eyes. His temperature is 37.3 C (99.1 F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 100/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows periorbital edema, but no erythema, no evidence of trauma, and no insect bite. Laboratory studies show:

Leukocyte count 8,500/mm3
Hemoglobin 13.5 mg/dL
Platelet count 400,000/mm3
Serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL
Serum albumin 2.0 g/dL
Cholesterol 210 mg/dL

Examination of a renal biopsy specimen shows normal-appearing glomeruli by light microscopy. Which of the following would most likely be found in the urine?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This patient has minimal change disease, which presents with nephrotic syndrome, is commonly seen in children, and is characterized by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria. Although not mentioned in the vignette, the condition can follow an upper respiratory tract infection, an allergic reaction to bee sting, or NSAID use. It is usually self-limited. However, some children require steroid therapy, where the condition usually resolves by puberty. Minimal change disease in adults can be associated with Hodgkin disease. Adults can respond to steroid treatment, although at a slower rate.

Light microscopy is normal, but diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes is seen by electron microscopy. This is attributed to an altered cell-mediated immunologic response with abnormal secretion of T cell lymphokines. This alters the foot processes, thereby causing reduced negative charge of the glomerular basement membrane, which decreases the ability to repel negatively charged albumin and results in selective proteinuria. In addition, nephrotic syndrome also presents with edema (hypoalbuminemia causes decreased intravascular oncotic pressure, causing fluids to shift into the interstitial space), hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria. There is also increased risk for thrombosis due to loss of antithrombin III (normally responsible for lysing thrombin and factor Xa; heparin and low molecular weight heparin potentiates effect of antithrombin III).

Granular casts (choice A) are comprised of dead, necrotic epithelial cells, and are seen in acute tubular necrosis (ATN), not minimal change disease. Ischemic or toxic injury to renal tubule epithelial cells cause the cells to slough off, form a mold within the renal tubule lumen, and are then flushed out in the urine.

Lambda light chains (choice B) are associated with multiple myeloma (Bence-Jones proteins), not minimal change disease. They are filtered through the glomeruli, accumulate in renal tubules, and cause proteinuria, tubular damage, and renal failure. Light chain nephropathy can, of course, present with nephrotic syndrome.

Neutrophils (choice D) can be seen with any bacterial urinary tract infection. Neutrophil casts reflect accumulation of neutrophils within renal tubule lumen, such as that seen in pyelonephritis, whereas scattered neutrophils in urine would be seen in lower locations such as ureter, bladder, and urethra.

Red blood cells (choice E) in urine (hematuria) are associated with conditions such as trauma, nephritic syndrome, bacterial infection (cystitis), and malignancies of the kidney and bladder. Red blood cell casts reflect accumulation of red cells within renal tubule lumen (nephritic syndrome), whereas scattered red blood cells would be extravasated within lower locations such as the ureter, bladder, and urethra.

choice_explanations.A: Granular casts (choice A) are comprised of dead, necrotic epithelial cells, and are seen in acute tubular necrosis (ATN), not minimal change disease. Ischemic or toxic injury to renal tubule epithelial cells cause the cells to slough off, form a mold within the renal tubule lumen, and are then flushed out in the urine.
choice_explanations.B: Lambda light chains (choice B) are associated with multiple myeloma (Bence-Jones proteins), not minimal change disease. They are filtered through the glomeruli, accumulate in renal tubules, and cause proteinuria, tubular damage, and renal failure. Light chain nephropathy can, of course, present with nephrotic syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome with massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria; lipids are the expected urinary finding.
choice_explanations.D: Neutrophils (choice D) can be seen with any bacterial urinary tract infection. Neutrophil casts reflect accumulation of neutrophils within renal tubule lumen, such as that seen in pyelonephritis, whereas scattered neutrophils in urine would be seen in lower locations such as ureter, bladder, and urethra.
choice_explanations.E: Red blood cells (choice E) in urine (hematuria) are associated with conditions such as trauma, nephritic syndrome, bacterial infection (cystitis), and malignancies of the kidney and bladder. Red blood cell casts reflect accumulation of red cells within renal tubule lumen (nephritic syndrome), whereas scattered red blood cells would be extravasated within lower locations such as the ureter, bladder, and urethra.

fa_summary: Nephrotic syndrome - Minimal change disease: normal glomeruli on light microscopy (lipid may be seen in PT cells), negative immunofluorescence, effacement of podocyte foot processes on EM; more common in children.

stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of progressive swelling in her feet. She attends dance class and is unable to participate along with the other children because of her condition. Physical examination reveals bilateral lower extremity edema from the ankles to the calves. A 24-hour urine collection reveals 4 grams of protein, but no red cells or casts. Kidney biopsy is performed and electron microscopy is utilized. Which of the following is the most likely finding on renal biopsy?

options.text: Diffuse effacement of epithelial foot processes

explanation:
The correct answer is B. Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by severe proteinuria (>3.5 g/d), hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, hyperlipidemia, and lipiduria. Minimal change disease (also called lipoid nephrosis and nil disease) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. The disease has peak incidence at ages 2 to 6. Light microscopy shows normal glomeruli with lipid accumulation in proximal tubule cells (lipoid nephrosis). Immunofluorescence is negative, with no immune deposits being visualized. Electron microscopy shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes but no immune complex deposits. The prognosis is excellent in children because treatment with corticosteroids produces a dramatic response. The majority have a complete recovery.

Other causes of nephrotic syndrome include focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and membranous nephropathy (also called membranous glomerulonephritis). Both are associated with visible glomerular pathology at the light microscopic level, unlike minimal change disease, which may appear essentially normal with light microscopy.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is a form of glomerular disease that affects both the glomerular mesangium and the basement membranes; it occurs in two types (type I and type II). Subendothelial deposits (choice D) are seen in type I MPGN. Dense deposits (choice A) within the glomerular basement membrane are seen in type II MPGN and described as intramembranous deposits.

Mesangial deposits (choice C) are a prominent feature of IgA nephropathy and are seen to a lesser degree in several other glomerulonephritides. IgA nephropathy can be associated with celiac sprue and Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

Subepithelial spikes (choice E) are a feature of membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN). Electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits along the basement membranes with effacement of podocyte foot processes. The "spikes" reflect the thin area of basement membrane that is present between the immune complex deposits. Immunofluorescence shows a granular and linear pattern of IgG and C3.

choice_explanations.A: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) occurs in two types (type I and type II). Dense deposits (choice A) within the glomerular basement membrane are seen in type II MPGN and described as intramembranous deposits.
choice_explanations.B: The correct answer is B. Electron microscopy in minimal change disease shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes but no immune complex deposits; light microscopy is normal.
choice_explanations.C: Mesangial deposits (choice C) are a prominent feature of IgA nephropathy and are seen to a lesser degree in several other glomerulonephritides. IgA nephropathy can be associated with celiac sprue and Henoch-Schonlein purpura.
choice_explanations.D: Subendothelial deposits (choice D) are seen in type I MPGN.
choice_explanations.E: Subepithelial spikes (choice E) are a feature of membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN). Electron microscopy shows subepithelial deposits along the basement membranes with effacement of podocyte foot processes. The "spikes" reflect the thin area of basement membrane that is present between the immune complex deposits. Immunofluorescence shows a granular and linear pattern of IgG and C3.

fa_summary: Nephrotic syndrome - Minimal change disease: light microscopy normal, immunofluorescence negative, electron microscopy shows effacement of podocyte foot processes; most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious at home. He regained consciousness in the ambulance and is able to state his name, date, and current year. He has no significant medical history. His temperature is 37 C (98.6 F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 80/45 mmHg. Physical examination shows no abrasions or bruises, non-tender abdomen, and normal reflexes. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin is 9 g/dL, hematocrit is 27%, and platelet count is 350,000/mm3. An upper GI endoscopy shows a bleeding duodenal ulcer, which is surgically repaired. He receives 6 units of packed red blood cells. Two days later, laboratory studies show:

Hemoglobin 15 g/dL
Hematocrit 45%
Serum urea nitrogen 35 mg/dL
Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL

Urine microscopy shows presence of granular casts and few red blood cells. Fractional excretion of sodium is 5.5% (normal 1-3%) and osmolality is 300 mosmol/kg H2O. Two weeks later at a post-discharge follow-up appointment, the urine sediment is clear and renal function is normal. Which of the following histologic features of the kidney would most likely be present in this patient at this time?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. The patient had acute tubular necrosis (ATN) from the hypotensive and hypovolemic episode. ATN can be caused by ischemic (hypotension, hemorrhage, sepsis) or nephrotoxic injury. The presence of elevated urea nitrogen, creatinine, granular casts, and elevated fractional excretion of sodium reflect the presence of ATN. ATN is reversible if treated and is fatal if untreated. When the patient's underlying condition is treated, recovery of the renal tissue can occur. The renal tubular epithelium can regenerate as long as the basement membrane is intact. In our patient, recovery and regeneration of tubular epithelium are reflected in the return of normal renal function and clear urine sediment.

Coagulative necrosis (choice A) is a form of necrosis where the cellular architecture is preserved ("ghost cells") for days to weeks. Occlusion of renal vessels leads to ischemia, resulting in coagulative necrosis. If extensive, patients would have hematuria and flank pain. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction that would lead to coagulative necrosis.

Fibrosis (choice B) and granulation tissue (choice C) are seen as part of wound healing from renal infarction associated with renal vessel occlusion (atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, hypertension) or thrombosis. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction.

Hemosiderosis (choice D) is accumulation of granular iron pigment within organs from a systemic overload of iron levels. Histologically, there would be brown pigment present in hepatocytes that would stain positive with Prussian blue iron stain. Causes of hemosiderosis include hereditary hemosiderosis, hemolytic anemia, and repeated red cell transfusions. Our patient had 6 units of red cell transfusion, which would not contribute to hemosiderosis. In contrast, local hemosiderin accumulation can be seen with bruising of an affected region, where macrophages would engulf extravasated red cells.

Occlusion of renal vessels leads to ischemia, resulting in coagulative necrosis. If extensive, patients would have hematuria and flank pain. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction that would lead to coagulative necrosis.
choice_explanations.B: Fibrosis (choice B) and granulation tissue (choice C) are seen as part of wound healing from renal infarction associated with renal vessel occlusion (atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, hypertension) or thrombosis. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction.
choice_explanations.C: Fibrosis (choice B) and granulation tissue (choice C) are seen as part of wound healing from renal infarction associated with renal vessel occlusion (atherosclerosis, diabetes mellitus, hypertension) or thrombosis. Our patient does not have any cause for renal infarction.
choice_explanations.D: Hemosiderosis (choice D) is accumulation of granular iron pigment within organs from a systemic overload of iron levels. Histologically, there would be brown pigment present in hepatocytes that would stain positive with Prussian blue iron stain. Causes of hemosiderosis include hereditary hemosiderosis, hemolytic anemia, and repeated red cell transfusions. Our patient had 6 units of red cell transfusion, which would not contribute to hemosiderosis. In contrast, local hemosiderin accumulation can be seen with bruising of an affected region, where macrophages would engulf extravasated red cells.
choice_explanations.E: The correct answer is E. The patient had acute tubular necrosis (ATN) from the hypotensive and hypovolemic episode. The renal tubular epithelium can regenerate as long as the basement membrane is intact; recovery and regeneration of tubular epithelium are reflected in the return of normal renal function and clear urine sediment.

fa_summary: Acute tubular necrosis: most common cause of intrinsic AKI; granular/muddy-brown casts; reversible - in the recovery phase the renal tubular epithelium regenerates as long as the basement membrane is intact.

stem: A 48-year-old man is brought to the physician because of persistent lower extremity edema. He says he has difficulty with ambulation. His pulse is 86/min and blood pressure is 100/64 mmHg. Cardiac and pulmonary examinations are noncontributory. Both lower extremities show pedal edema that tracks superiorly to the level of the knee. The left leg is slightly more swollen and erythematous with a positive Homans sign. Urinalysis reveals +2 blood, +4 proteinuria, and is negative for nitrates and leukocyte esterase. Microscopy reveals few red blood cells. Renal biopsy confirms glomerular inflammation and thickened basement membranes. Which of the following substances is most likely to be elevated in this patient's plasma?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Nephrotic syndrome is the clinical state in which patients have massive proteinuria resulting in generalized edema (due to decreased plasma oncotic pressure from albumin loss) and hyperlipidemia with fatty casts in the urine. Diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome is made by finding >3.5 g/day of protein in the urine. Here, urinalysis (urine dipstick) results indicate 4+ protein, which correlates to 3.5 g protein/day. Massive protein loss is thought to stimulate increased hepatic lipoprotein production resulting in increased levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Patients with nephrotic syndrome have changes in their lipoprotein metabolism and the underlying mechanism is not clearly understood. Elevated levels of LDL, IDL, VLDL, and Lp(a) are seen, but levels of HDL are normal or low. In addition, the composition of the lipoproteins are altered with a higher ratio of cholesterol to triglycerides in the apo-B-containing lipoproteins. ApoC III to apoC II ratio is also increased (apoC II activates LPL, while apoC III inhibits LPL), which may contribute to lipoprotein catabolism in nephrotic syndrome. Conditions that cause nephrotic syndrome include focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS; most common), membranous glomerulopathy, membranoproliferative glomerulopathy, diabetes mellitus, amyloidosis, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In this case we cannot identify the causative condition.

For urinalysis (urine dipstick) result interpretation: "0" is normal baseline, mild values are 1-2+, and severe values are 3-4+. This patient has 2+ blood on the dipstick and few red blood cells in the urine microscopy, indicating mild hematuria, which can be present in nephrotic syndrome due to glomerular basement membrane dysfunction (e.g., membranous glomerulonephropathy). As a general rule, when there is more proteinuria than hematuria, think nephrotic syndrome, and vice versa for nephritic syndrome. Similar results (4+ protein and 4+ blood) may indicate a combined nephrotic and nephritic syndrome presentation. Note: Minimal change disease only has proteinuria. The clinical finding of hypotension further suggests the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome (decreased oncotic pressure).

Interestingly, HDL levels (choice D) are not generally affected and do not increase. Other important plasma proteins that are lost in the urine of patients with nephrotic syndrome include immunoglobulins (resulting in increased risk of infections) and antithrombin III (resulting in a hypercoagulable state and increased risk of thromboembolism). In addition to albumin, the glomerular capillary wall also becomes permeable to lipid, producing lipiduria.

choice_explanations.B: Ammonia is not characteristically elevated in nephrotic syndrome.
choice_explanations.C: Glucose is not characteristically elevated in nephrotic syndrome (this patient's fasting glucose history is unremarkable).
choice_explanations.D: Interestingly, HDL levels (choice D) are not generally affected and do not increase.
choice_explanations.E: The correct answer is E. Massive protein loss is thought to stimulate increased hepatic lipoprotein production resulting in increased levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood; elevated levels of LDL, IDL, VLDL, and Lp(a) are seen in nephrotic syndrome.
choice_explanations.F: Potassium is not characteristically elevated in nephrotic syndrome.

fa_summary: Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), edema, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia from increased hepatic lipogenesis, fatty casts, hypercoagulable state (antithrombin loss).

stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the physician for follow-up examination because of sickle cell disease. She has a history of multiple admissions to the hospital because of sickle cell crises. Her crises are usually precipitated by upper respiratory infections and urinary infections. Physical examination is unremarkable except for mild edema around the eyes. Urine analysis reveals 2+ blood, 3+ protein, and negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Urine microscopy reveals increased red cells, few degenerated epithelial cells, and no leukocytes or casts. Pyelography with contrast material demonstrates bilateral deformities of the renal papillae. Which of the following renal structures are most likely to be damaged in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient has sickle cell nephropathy. Sickling crises can be triggered by hypoxia caused by high altitude or pneumonia. The renal medulla is supplied by the vasa recta. The very high osmolarity and hypoxic environment of the renal medulla, along with slow blood flow in the vasa recta, cause sickling of erythrocytes. The resultant ischemia can cause a patchy papillary necrosis, hematuria, proteinuria, and sometimes cortical scarring.

Larger blood vessels such as the arcuate arteries (choice A), interlobular arteries (choice C), and renal arteries (choice D) are usually not occluded by sickled cells.

The glomerular capillaries (choice B) are small enough to be occluded by sickled cells but they are well oxygenated and the fluid within them is not hypertonic, so the glomerular capillaries are significantly less likely to become occluded than the vasa recta.

stem:
A 66-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unconscious after being found lying on the floor in his kitchen. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is begun. Laboratory analysis of an arterial blood sample obtained upon admission shows:

Plasma pH 7.19
Plasma [HCO3-] 15 mEq/L
Arterial PCO2 50 mm Hg
Arterial PO2 80 mm Hg
SaO2 (pulse oximetry) 88%
Plasma Na+ 142 mEq/L
Plasma K+ 4.8 mEq/L
Plasma Cl- 102 mEq/L
Serum lactate 6.1 mmol/L

Which of the following types of acid-base abnormality is most likely present in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. A mixed acidosis commonly occurs with cardiopulmonary arrest. Cardiac arrest patients experience at least some degree of lactic acidosis (metabolic acidosis) as a result of poorly perfused tissues. Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis should reduce arterial PCO2, but simultaneous respiratory acidosis due to ventilatory standstill also occurs during cardiac arrest. This combination of metabolic acidosis and respiratory acidosis is referred to as a "mixed acidosis."

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation shows the relationship between PCO2, bicarbonate, and pH. One common form of this equation is pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3-]/(0.03 x PCO2). While it is unlikely that the USMLE will require calculation of pH, understanding the relationship shown by this equation is essential. The key is that the ratio of HCO3-/PCO2 determines the pH. Decreased HCO3- or increased PCO2 decreases the pH. Lactic acidosis caused by cardiac arrest is buffered by bicarbonate, so the bicarbonate level decreases. The simultaneous respiratory arrest increases arterial PCO2, which is converted to carbonic acid, thus exacerbating the acidotic state; clinically, lower than normal arterial pH is called acidemia. The normal value of pH is 7.40 (reference range 7.35-7.45). Although he is being resuscitated, his arterial blood gases have not normalized, and lactic acid is nonvolatile, so it is more slowly cleared from the body. His lactate is elevated, and his plasma anion gap [calculated as [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-])] equals 25 mEq/L, which is grossly elevated (reference range = 8-16 mEq/L). These findings confirm metabolic acidosis.

A metabolic acidosis (choice A) is present when plasma pH and HCO3- concentration are low. Respiratory compensation is increased ventilation triggered by acidemia; respiratory compensation would reduce arterial PCO2, but this patient's is high.

Metabolic alkalosis (choice B) is diagnosed by an abnormal increase of bicarbonate; this patient's bicarbonate is low.

Mixed alkalosis (choice D) is metabolic alkalosis (higher than normal bicarbonate) with lower than normal PCO2; neither finding describes this patient.

Respiratory acidosis (choice E) is present when plasma pH is low and arterial CO2 is high. Respiratory acidosis itself will slightly increase arterial bicarbonate when carbonic acid breaks down into H+ and bicarbonate. Metabolic compensation would have increased bicarbonate above the amount caused by respiratory acidosis. This patient's bicarbonate was very low. Also, metabolic compensation for respiratory acidosis requires at least one day.

Respiratory alkalosis (choice F) is caused by increased ventilation. It is characterized by low arterial PCO2; this patient's PCO2 was high. Metabolic compensation for respiratory alkalosis is to decrease bicarbonate level, i.e., compensatory metabolic acidosis.

choice_explanations.B: Metabolic alkalosis (choice B) is diagnosed by an abnormal increase of bicarbonate; this patient's bicarbonate is low.
choice_explanations.C: The correct answer is C. This combination of metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis from poorly perfused tissues) and respiratory acidosis (ventilatory standstill) is a "mixed acidosis."
choice_explanations.D: Mixed alkalosis (choice D) is metabolic alkalosis (higher than normal bicarbonate) with lower than normal PCO2; neither finding describes this patient.

Also, metabolic compensation for respiratory acidosis requires at least one day.

stem: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the physician for follow-up. She has had difficulties with swallowing and feeding since birth. Physical examination shows weakness of the extremities, nystagmus, and a weak cry. MRI shows a small posterior fossa, downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis, cerebellar tonsils, and medulla through the foramen magnum, and a fluid-filled cavity in the cervical cord. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. This patient has a Chiari II malformation as evidenced by the downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis, cerebellar tonsils, and medulla through the foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal. This malformation obstructs the outflow of CSF in the posterior fossa, causing hydrocephalus in most patients. Chiari type II is invariably associated with a myelomeningocele, a cleft in the vertebral column (usually lumbosacral) that allows the spinal cord and meninges to protrude through as shown in the figure below. Syringomyelia (the development of a fluid-filled cavity or syrinx in the spinal cord) also commonly occurs in Chiari II malformations and presents with chronic pain and sensory/motor disturbances primarily in the upper extremities. Although Chiari I malformation is also associated with herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, this child is unlikely to have this condition. Chiari I is a more common, but less severe, condition that is often diagnosed in adults and adolescents; it can sometimes be an incidental finding on radiography. Chiari II is less common and more severe, and is more typically diagnosed in infants and young children.

Agenesis of the corpus callosum (choice A) is a rare congenital disorder in which there is partial or complete absence of the corpus callosum. It can occur in isolation or in combination with other abnormalities, including Chiari malformation and Dandy-Walker syndrome. Although it can occur with both Chiari I and Chiari II malformations, it is infrequent. Remember, the USMLE often asks for the most likely answer, and there may be some answers that are partially correct, but not the best answer. Meningomyelocele is by far the best answer in this case.

Ependymoma of the 4th ventricle (choice B) is a glial tumor that arises from ependymal cells in the 4th ventricle. In children, approximately 90% of ependymomas are intracranial, and most arise from the roof of the 4th ventricle. Obstructive hydrocephalus can occur, but herniation does not. It is in the differential for Chiari II, but is not itself associated with it.

Holoprosencephaly (choice C) results from incomplete separation of the cerebral hemispheres along the midline, leading, in its extreme form, to a single midline ventricular cavity enclosed within the forebrain. Associated facial anomalies, including cyclopia (a single midline eye in the forehead with associated proboscis), are frequent. Holoprosencephaly is often associated with trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome) and less often with trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome). It is not associated with Chiari II malformation.

Lissencephaly (choice D) means "smooth brain" and results from defective neuronal migration resulting in a lack of brain gyri (folds) and sulci (grooves). This is not associated with Chiari II malformation. In fact, polymicrogyria (excessive number of small gyri on the brain surface) can be associated with Chiari II.

Myelomeningocele is a cleft in the vertebral column (usually lumbosacral) that allows the spinal cord and meninges to protrude through. It is invariably associated with Chiari type II malformation, making E the best answer.

Spinal astrocytomas (choice F) are rare tumors that arise from spinal cord astrocytes in adult and pediatric populations. Patients generally present with symptoms at or below the level of the spinal cord tumor. Spinal astrocytoma is part of the differential diagnosis for Chiari II, but is not associated with it.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because of a seizure. Her daughter states that she has complained of headaches over the last couple of weeks and she has episodes of confusion. A CT scan of the head shows a left temporal lobe mass with subfalcine herniation. She undergoes surgical resection and a frozen section shows bizarre pleomorphic tumor cells accompanied by necrosis and hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most aggressive tumor in the astrocytic line and is the most common CNS primary malignancy in adults (typical age is over 50 years of age). It can also occur in children, often in the brainstem. GBM tends to be a tumor of the cerebral cortex in adults. Histologically, the tumor tends to show necrosis and hemorrhage. The tumor cells are pleomorphic, and frequently are bizarre in appearance with markedly enlarged, abnormal nuclei. The characteristic histopathologic feature (as shown in the figure below) is an area of necrosis surrounded by rows of neoplastic cells [pseudopalisading necrosis].

Craniopharyngiomas (choice A) are cystic tumors derived from remnants of the craniopharyngeal duct and/or Rathke's cleft. They are usually located in the suprasellar or sellar region, and may produce visual deficits. Craniopharyngiomas are composed of squamous epithelium, often with a papillary architecture. One type resembles an adamantinoma (the most common type of tooth tumor).

Ependymomas (choice B), in this age group, commonly arise from the fourth ventricle. These present as papillary masses, characteristically with perivascular rosettes. They can produce hydrocephalus by obstructing the flow of CSF.

Fibrillary astrocytoma (choice C) represents a well-differentiated variant of astrocytic tumors, whereas glioblastoma multiforme is a poorly differentiated one.

Glioblastoma multiforme is the most aggressive tumor in the astrocytic line and is the most common CNS primary malignancy in adults. Histologically it shows necrosis and hemorrhage with bizarre pleomorphic tumor cells and pseudopalisading necrosis, matching the frozen section in this patient.

Oligodendrogliomas (choice E) and pilocytic astrocytomas (choice F) do not usually show pleomorphism, necrosis, or hemorrhage. The classic histologic description for oligodendrogliomas includes a "fried egg" appearance in which the nuclei are surrounded by clear cytoplasm. There is also a prominence of fine capillary network admixed within the tumor. Rosenthal fibers are a classic finding in pilocytic astrocytoma.

There is also a prominence of fine capillary network admixed within the tumor. Rosenthal fibers are a classic finding in pilocytic astrocytoma.

FA table also contrasts oligodendroglioma (calcified, frontal lobes, 'fried egg'), meningioma, and childhood tumors.

stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of stumbling and falls. She has a broad-based, slow, clumsy gait with a tendency to lurch from side to side. Several years later, she develops clumsiness of fine movements and a coarse intention tremor of the upper limbs. Her illness progresses slowly to kyphoscoliosis and foot deformities. She eventually becomes bedridden and dies in the fourth decade of life from congestive heart failure. Which of the following neurologic findings is most likely on autopsy?

options.text: Selective frontal and temporal lobe atrophy

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The disease is Friedreich ataxia, which is an autosomal recessive degenerative disorder and is the most common hereditary ataxia. This disease is caused by a mutation in the frataxin (FXN) gene on chromosome 9, which codes for the mitochondrial protein, frataxin. The majority of these patients have an expanded trinucleotide (GAA) repeat in this gene, which leads to decreased expression of frataxin, an iron-binding protein. One theory is that decreased frataxin levels produce mitochondrial iron overload, leading to oxidative stress. Degeneration of large myelinated axons in peripheral nerves, posterior (dorsal) columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts occurs, causing the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia to atrophy. The cerebellum also degenerates to a lesser extent. Symptoms typically appear between age 5 and 15, and begin with a gait ataxia and eventually spread to the arms and trunk. Eventually, patients become wheelchair-bound, and finally, bedridden. As the disease progresses, dysarthria and dysphagia occur. Speech becomes incomprehensible and because of incoordination of breathing, speaking, and swallowing, patients can nearly choke while speaking. Scoliosis and foot deformities are frequent findings and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy occurs in over 50% of patients. No treatment is known that can alter the course of this devastating disease. Most patients die from cardiac causes (e.g., CHF, arrhythmias) between the ages of 30 to 40.

Atrophy of the caudate (choice A) is seen in Huntington disease, which is characterized by choreoathetosis, dementia, and eventual death. This autosomal dominant disorder is caused by a CAG repeat, and typically does not present until midlife.

Friedreich ataxia causes degeneration of large myelinated axons in peripheral nerves, posterior (dorsal) columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts, causing the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia to atrophy; this matches the clinical picture.

Depigmentation of the substantia nigra (choice C) is seen in Parkinson disease, a hypokinetic movement disorder characterized by rigidity, bradykinesia, and a slow resting tremor.

Diffuse cortical atrophy (choice D) is seen in Alzheimer disease, a cause of dementia in the aged population.

Selective frontal and temporal lobe atrophy (choice E) is seen in Pick disease, a severe dementing disease presenting in older populations.

choice_explanations.A: Atrophy of the caudate (choice A) is seen in Huntington disease, which is characterized by choreoathetosis, dementia, and eventual death. This autosomal dominant disorder is caused by a CAG repeat, and typically does not present until midlife.
choice_explanations.B: Friedreich ataxia causes degeneration of large myelinated axons in peripheral nerves, posterior (dorsal) columns, spinocerebellar tracts, and corticospinal tracts, causing the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia to atrophy; this matches the clinical picture.
choice_explanations.C: Depigmentation of the substantia nigra (choice C) is seen in Parkinson disease, a hypokinetic movement disorder characterized by rigidity, bradykinesia, and a slow resting tremor.
choice_explanations.D: Diffuse cortical atrophy (choice D) is seen in Alzheimer disease, a cause of dementia in the aged population.
choice_explanations.E: Selective frontal and temporal lobe atrophy (choice E) is seen in Pick disease, a severe dementing disease presenting in older populations.

stem: An autopsy is performed on a 60-year-old man who develops visual hallucinations, fluctuating dementia, and eventual parkinsonism. Histopathologic examination shows numerous eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions within neurons of the substantia nigra, limbic cortex, and basal nucleus of Meynert. The inclusions are immunoreactive for ubiquitin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This question focuses on neurodegenerative and dementing illnesses. The correct answer can be deduced by combining clinical and pathologic features. Diffuse Lewy body disease (dementia with Lewy bodies) is characterized by widespread formation of Lewy bodies (intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions), containing alpha-synuclein or ubiquitin within neurons of the substantia nigra (producing parkinsonism), cholinergic nuclei such as the basal nucleus of Meynert (producing dementia), and limbic cortex (which may explain the hallucinations). Once believed to be infrequent, recent clinicopathologic investigations have suggested that this might be one of the most frequent causes of dementia in industrialized countries, perhaps second only to Alzheimer disease. Peculiar to this dementing disorder is the presence of extrapyramidal symptoms and visual hallucinations, together with an undulating clinical course.

Alzheimer disease (choice A) is the most common neurodegenerative disease that results in dementia (accounting for about half of all cases of dementia) and is characterized by high numbers of senile plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the hippocampus, neocortex, and cholinergic nuclei of the basal forebrain. There is no involvement of the substantia nigra and thus no extrapyramidal symptoms. Visual hallucinations, parkinsonian motor features, and cognitive fluctuations help to distinguish AD from Lewy body dementia.

ALS (choice B) can be ruled out because of the clinical picture. ALS is caused by degeneration of motor neurons in the anterior horns of the spinal cord (lower motor neurons; causing atrophy and fasciculations) and/or large pyramidal neurons in the primary motor cortex (upper motor neurons; causing spastic paresis and hyperreflexia). This condition thus manifests with progressive weakness involving lower and upper extremities. Bulbar muscles are also similarly affected. Skeletal muscles become atrophic (hence the term amyotrophic) and show a denervation pattern on biopsy.

Diffuse Lewy body disease (dementia with Lewy bodies) is characterized by widespread formation of Lewy bodies (intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions) containing alpha-synuclein or ubiquitin within neurons of the substantia nigra, cholinergic nuclei such as the basal nucleus of Meynert, and limbic cortex, producing parkinsonism, dementia, and visual hallucinations with an undulating course.

Parkinson disease (choice D) is caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and manifests with tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia. A subset of patients who have Parkinson disease develops dementia. Parkinson disease thus may be difficult to differentiate from dementia with Lewy bodies. Patients with Parkinson disease dementia typically have a diagnosis of Parkinson disease for over a year, then later develop dementia. Lewy bodies are typically absent in cortical regions of patients who have classic Parkinson disease.

Pick disease (choice E) is the most frequent of dementing disorders in the category of frontotemporal dementia. This condition leads to extreme atrophy of frontal and temporal cortex, with relative sparing of the remaining neocortical regions. Neocortical neurons bear round intracytoplasmic inclusions known as Pick bodies, which contain altered neurofilaments, tau, and ubiquitin. No inclusions are found in the substantia nigra.

There is no involvement of the substantia nigra and thus no extrapyramidal symptoms. Visual hallucinations, parkinsonian motor features, and cognitive fluctuations help to distinguish AD from Lewy body dementia.

stem: An 80-year-old woman dies after a long history of progressive memory loss, apraxia, and recurrent episodes of confusion. In the last months of life, she was bedridden and unable to recognize familiar faces and objects. Microscopic examination of brain tissue obtained at autopsy shows numerous flame-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions in neurons of the neocortex and hippocampus. Electron microscopy shows that the inclusions consist of paired helical filaments. Which of the following is most likely involved in the development of the intracytoplasmic aggregates in this condition?

options.text: Abnormal degradation of amyloid precursor protein (APP)
Accumulation of advanced glycosylation end (AGE) products
GAA repeats in a gene encoding a mitochondrial protein

explanation:
The correct answer is B. This patient has all of the characteristic clinical features of dementia (memory loss, apraxia, and confusion). Alzheimer disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly. Gross findings in AD include cortical atrophy, widening of cerebral sulci, ventricular enlargement (hydrocephalus ex vacuo, due to loss of brain tissue), and atrophy of the medial temporal lobe (hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, amygdala). The major microscopic findings include neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), which are intracellular, and neuritic (senile) plaques, which are extracellular plaques of amyloid. As described in our case, NFTs are bundles of insoluble fibers that accumulate in the neuronal cytoplasm, particularly in the medial temporal lobe. As the disease progresses, they accumulate in other cortical regions, especially higher order association cortex. The primary constituent of NFTs is the microtubule-associated protein, tau. Normally, tau binds to and stabilizes microtubules, thus aiding in the neuronal transport system. In AD, tau becomes hyperphosphorylated, cannot bind microtubules, and instead forms insoluble paired helical filaments (PHF), which are the primary components of NFTs, leading to the collapse of the neuron's transport system (see image). (Note: if you knew that intracellular NFTs are associated with Alzheimer's and that tau is an important component of NFTs, you did not need to know the exact mechanism to arrive at the correct answer.) Senile plaques are dense extracellular deposits of protein and cellular material associated with microglia and astrocytes. The primary component of the plaque core is beta amyloid (Aβ), a peptide derived from a larger molecule, amyloid precursor protein (APP). The APP gene is on chromosome 21, which explains why patients with Down syndrome develop AD in their 40s (due to the extra dose of the APP gene).

Degradation of APP (choice A) leads to formation of beta-amyloid (Aβ), a component of extracellular senile plaques, not the neurofibrillary tangles.

The primary constituent of neurofibrillary tangles is the microtubule-associated protein tau. In AD, tau becomes hyperphosphorylated, cannot bind microtubules, and instead forms insoluble paired helical filaments, matching the flame-shaped inclusions and paired helical filaments in this patient.

Advanced glycosylation end (AGE) products (choice C) are insoluble proteins (mostly collagen and other long-lived proteins) that accumulate progressively in vessel walls as a result of glycosylation. This is a mechanism underlying damage in diabetes mellitus and aging but not in the formation of neurofibrillary tangles.

PrPᶜ (choice D) is the beta-pleated sheet conformation of PrPᶜ, a protein normally present in neurons. PrPᶜ is a prion protein responsible for the cerebral pathologic changes (usually resulting in spongiform changes) in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

GAA repeats in the frataxin gene, which encodes a mitochondrial protein (choice E), are thought to be responsible for the development of Friedreich ataxia. The frataxin protein is necessary for mitochondrial iron regulation. Mutations in frataxin produce increases in mitochondrial iron, leading to free radical damage and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Mutation of the gene encoding zinc-copper superoxide dismutase (choice F) is thought to underlie some hereditary cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). ALS is primarily a motor disease, although it can occasionally produce frontotemporal dementia.

In AD, tau becomes hyperphosphorylated, cannot bind microtubules, and instead forms insoluble paired helical filaments, matching the flame-shaped inclusions and paired helical filaments in this patient.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of a stroke comes to the physician for physical therapy. Physical examination shows hyperreflexia of the patellar tendon tap. The spasticity reflects loss of inhibitory influences that normally limit responses to afferent signals that convey information about muscle length. Which of the following structures within the muscle actively initiates the abnormally brisk patellar reflex arc in this patient?
explanation:
The correct answer is E. Several mechanisms contribute to the regulation of muscle length. Spindle afferents and other sensory fibers attached to the intrafusal fibers detect changes in length of the muscle by detecting tension of the intrafusal fibers. When the patellar tendon is tapped, the muscle is stretched. The increased length is detected by the spindle afferents, which synapse with and activate the alpha motor neurons that innervate the muscle. The stretch of the muscle thereby initiates contraction of the muscle to shorten it to its initial length. Hyperreflexia is a sign that upper motor neuron pathways that inhibit activity have been lost, thus allowing excessive response to movement: the classical definition of spasticity is velocity-dependent spasms.

Alpha motor neurons (choice A) carry motor impulses in a reflex arc in response to afferent information from intrafusal fiber stretch via the Ia nerves. They do not inherently modulate muscle tension.

Extrafusal fibers (choice B) constitute the bulk of the contracting muscle belly. They produce, but do not modulate, muscle tension.

Golgi tendon organs (choice C) are not responsible for the myotactic reflexes, such as the tendon tap. They regulate muscle tension and are involved in fine control of movement and control of posture.

Intrafusal fibers (choice D) are the filaments to which the spindle afferents are attached. When the muscle as a whole is stretched, the intrafusal fibers are also stretched. They themselves are not the sensor; the sensors are several types of proprioceptors that are attached to them. In response to stretch, spindle afferents produce impulses via the Ia fibers that stimulate alpha motor neurons and muscle contraction. Intrafusal fibers can modulate the signal sent by spindle afferents when the gamma efferents cause their contraction.

Spindle afferents and other sensory fibers attached to the intrafusal fibers detect changes in muscle length by detecting tension of the intrafusal fibers; on tendon tap they are the sensor that initiates the stretch (deep tendon) reflex, making E the answer.

stem: A 55-year-old woman comes to the physician because of worsening headaches. A CT of the head shows a well-circumscribed mass in the right cerebral hemisphere. Biopsy of the mass shows neoplastic cells with round nuclei and clear cytoplasm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is D. Oligodendroglioma has a "fried egg" appearance, tumor cells with round nuclei (the "yolk") and cleared cytoplasm (the "white"). These tumors may contain areas of calcification, hemorrhage, or cysts. They tend to occur in the cerebral hemispheres of middle-aged patients of both sexes, and have a better prognosis (average survival 5 years) than astrocytomas.

Choroid plexus papilloma (choice A) is a benign papillary growth in a ventricle.

Ependymoma (choice B): small uniform cells arranged in true rosettes and pseudorosettes patterns, with structures resembling ependymal canals. Tumors arise in the cerebral hemisphere.

Glioblastoma multiforme (choice C) has extreme pleomorphism, necrosis, and hemorrhage. Tumors arise in the cerebral hemisphere and can infiltrate along white matter.

Oligodendroglioma shows a "fried egg" appearance with round nuclei surrounded by clear cytoplasm, typically in the cerebral hemispheres of middle-aged patients, matching this biopsy.

Pilocytic astrocytoma (choice E) is a low-grade tumor composed of bipolar cells associated with Rosenthal fibers, and arises in the cerebellum of young children. Other types of astrocytoma affect adults and are located in the cortex.

choice_explanations.A: Choroid plexus papilloma (choice A) is a benign papillary growth in a ventricle.
choice_explanations.B: Ependymoma (choice B): small uniform cells arranged in true rosettes and pseudorosettes patterns, with structures resembling ependymal canals. Tumors arise in the cerebral hemisphere.
choice_explanations.C: Glioblastoma multiforme (choice C) has extreme pleomorphism, necrosis, and hemorrhage. Tumors arise in the cerebral hemisphere and can infiltrate along white matter.
choice_explanations.D: Oligodendroglioma shows a "fried egg" appearance with round nuclei surrounded by clear cytoplasm, typically in the cerebral hemispheres of middle-aged patients, matching this biopsy.
choice_explanations.E: Pilocytic astrocytoma (choice E) is a low-grade tumor composed of bipolar cells associated with Rosenthal fibers, and arises in the cerebellum of young children. Other types of astrocytoma affect adults and are located in the cortex.

fa_summary: Oligodendroglioma: relatively rare, slow-growing, most often in frontal lobes/cerebral hemispheres, often calcified; oligodendrocyte origin; histology has a 'fried egg' appearance with round nuclei and clear cytoplasm and a fine capillary network.

stem: A 39-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of headaches. She has no history of major medical illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. A head CT shows a mass above the left petrous bone. A biopsy specimen shows a malignant schwannoma on the left trigeminal nerve. The patient undergoes surgery for resection of the mass. Which of the following is most likely to be found on examination if there is damage to the nerve during the surgery?

options.text: Decreased accommodation of the left eye
Decreased corneal reflex of the left eye
Decreased taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Inability to adduct the left eye

explanation:
The correct answer is B. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is a mixed (sensory and motor) nerve. It provides sensory innervation to the face, cornea, mucous membranes of the nasal and oral cavities, frontal sinus, anterior two-thirds of the tongue, teeth, and hard palate. It also provides motor innervation for the muscles of mastication (i.e., temporalis, masseter, lateral and medial pterygoids), anterior belly of the digastric, tensor tympani, tensor palati, and the mylohyoid muscles. If this patient's left CN V was lesioned during surgery, she could lose the corneal (blink) reflex on the left. The corneal reflex is elicited by stimulation of the cornea (such as with cotton) and results in both a direct (ipsilateral) and consensual (contralateral) blink response. The afferent (sensory) limb is transmitted by CN V (unilateral) and the efferent (motor) limb (bilateral) is transmitted by the facial nerve (CN VII). Additional symptoms that the patient could also have include left facial anesthesia, ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of muscles of mastication, deviation of the jaw to the left, paralysis of the tensor tympani muscle (causing hypoacusis), and trigeminal neuralgia.

Accommodation (choice A) involves many structures, such as CN III, the superior colliculus, and the pretectal nucleus. CN V is not involved in accommodation.

The corneal (blink) reflex has its afferent (sensory) limb carried by CN V; a left trigeminal lesion abolishes the left corneal reflex, so this is the most likely finding.

The gag reflex (choice C) is a reflex contraction of the back of the throat that is elicited by touching the back of the mouth and throat. This reflex involves only CN IX (afferent, unilateral) and CN X (efferent, bilateral). CN V does not provide sensory function in this area and is not involved in this reflex.

Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (choice D) is transmitted by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (CN VII). CN V carries general somatic information from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but not taste.

Adduction of the left eye (choice E) is controlled by the oculomotor nerve (CN III) via the action of the medial rectus.

choice_explanations.A: Accommodation (choice A) involves many structures, such as CN III, the superior colliculus, and the pretectal nucleus. CN V is not involved in accommodation.
choice_explanations.B: The corneal (blink) reflex has its afferent (sensory) limb carried by CN V; a left trigeminal lesion abolishes the left corneal reflex, so this is the most likely finding.
choice_explanations.C: The gag reflex (choice C) is a reflex contraction of the back of the throat that is elicited by touching the back of the mouth and throat. This reflex involves only CN IX (afferent, unilateral) and CN X (efferent, bilateral). CN V does not provide sensory function in this area and is not involved in this reflex.
choice_explanations.D: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (choice D) is transmitted by the chorda tympani of the facial nerve (CN VII). CN V carries general somatic information from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but not taste.
choice_explanations.E: Adduction of the left eye (choice E) is controlled by the oculomotor nerve (CN III) via the action of the medial rectus.

stem: A stillborn male at 30 weeks gestation age has multiple physical deformities. He has microcephaly, a cleft lip, cleft palate, and eyes that are very small, with fissures of the iris, shallow supraorbital ridges, and slanted palpebral fissures. His ears are low-set and malformed. Each hand has six fingers and a simian crease. Which of the following is most likely associated with this congenital disorder?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. This is the typical presentation of trisomy 13, also known as Patau syndrome. Affected infants usually die before 1 year of age, usually secondary to multiple congenital anomalies, particularly severe congenital renal and heart defects (VSD most common). Other features include holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia, microcephaly, cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, congenital heart disease, and severe mental retardation. A useful mnemonic for Patau syndrome is M1CROCePHaly: Mental retardation, 13 chromosome, Cardiac defects, Renal defects, Cleft lip & palate, Polydactyly, Holoprosencephaly. Note: simian crease, as seen in our patient, can also be seen in Down syndrome. Holoprosencephaly is characterized by the incomplete separation of the cerebral hemispheres, with lack of midline cranial structures such as the corpus callosum and thalamus. Severe forms have midline facial abnormalities, such as cyclopia.

Anencephaly (choice A) is a form of neural tube defect, associated with folate deficiency, and is characterized by complete failure of higher brain structures to develop. There is a grossly deformed head with virtually no cranial vault. It is not associated with Patau syndrome.

Encephalocele (choice B) is a form of neural tube defect, associated with folate deficiency, and is characterized by a protrusion of brain and meninges through a developmental defect in the skull most commonly in the occipital region. It is not associated with Patau syndrome.

Holoprosencephaly, from failure of the forebrain to divide into two cerebral hemispheres, is a classic finding in Patau syndrome (trisomy 13), matching this infant's microcephaly, midline facial clefts, microphthalmia, and polydactyly.

Lissencephaly (choice D), also known as agyria, is a forebrain anomaly characterized by the absence of cortical gyri. Grossly, the fetal cortex has a smooth surface and lacks the normal gyri. It is not associated with Patau syndrome.

Polymicrogyria (choice E) is characterized by multiple, small irregularly-formed cortical convolutions. This condition may be sporadic (prenatal injury to tissue during neuronal migration) or genetic. However, polymicrogyria is not associated with Patau syndrome.

There is a grossly deformed head with virtually no cranial vault. It is not associated with Patau syndrome.

stem: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician because of tingling and weakness in the arms. He denies any recent syncope, fall, or trauma, but describes increased episodes of burning his fingers and hands while cooking lately. There is no significant past medical history. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows some atrophy of the small muscles of the hands, but no motor deficits in the lower extremities. There is absence of pain and temperature sensation in both arms, shoulders, and upper chest, but intact touch, position, and vibratory sensations. Deep tendon reflex is 1+ in biceps brachii, brachioradialis, and triceps brachii. Which of the following findings would most likely be present on the MRI of the head and spine?

options.text: Demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns
Hyperintense demyelinating plaques in the white matter
Lacunar infarcts in the thalamus and basal ganglia
Syrinx within the cervical spinal cord
Tumor metastasis to the spinal cord

explanation:
The correct answer is D. The patient has syringomyelia, which is the development of a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within spinal cord that usually involves the cervical region. Interruption of spinothalamic decussation (in the anterior white commissure) can result in decreased pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution across shoulders, arms and upper torso (cape distribution). Light touch, vibration, and position sensory are preserved (dissociated sensory loss). As the cavitation expands, lower motor neurons in the ventral horn may be affected and can cause atrophy of hand muscles, which can progress to the forearms and shoulders. Growing cavitation can also involve the corticospinal tracts, leading to upper motor neuron signs. Syringomyelia can arise from different causes: idiopathic, Arnold-Chiari malformation, tumor (meningioma, ependymoma, or other tumors).

Demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns (choice A) reflects vitamin B12 deficiency-associated myelopathy. Demyelination usually occurs in the white matter of the upper thoracic spinal cord. Lesions can spread laterally and cranially to the corticospinal tracts in the cervical segments. These patients can present with myelopathy and/or neuropathy. Typically, there is initial loss of position and vibration sensation, which can progress to loss of light touch, pinprick, and temperature sensation; legs are affected before the arms. Wide-based gait, muscle atrophy and decreased reflexes are present. Our patient has intact position and vibration sensation.

Hyperintense demyelinating plaques in the white matter (choice B) describe multiple sclerosis (MS), a CNS immune-mediated neurodegenerative condition. MRI scan is the most sensitive diagnostic test to identify demyelinating lesions in the brain and spinal cord. MS usually affects females > males. Patients may present with cognitive changes, paresthesia (sensory loss, particularly to vibration and position), poor coordination, hyperreflexia, spasticity, diplopia, optic neuritis, and autonomic dysfunction (bowel, bladder, sexual dysfunction). These features are not present in our patient.

Lacunar infarcts in the thalamus and basal ganglia (choice C) are small subcortical ischemic infarcts that result from occlusion in the deep penetrating arteries (basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule) and are associated with chronic hypertension, diabetes mellitus, tobacco smoking, or microembolism (from atrial fibrillation or carotid arteries). These vessels are usually not affected by atherosclerosis, but may develop microatheroma, lipohyalinosis, and aneurysm formation (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms). Signs and symptoms vary, depending upon what structures are affected: motor (paresis) or sensory (paresthesia) dysfunction. Our patient does not have hypertension and unilateral neurologic deficits.

Syringomyelia is a fluid-filled, gliosis-lined cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord that usually involves the cervical region; it interrupts spinothalamic decussation, producing cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch/vibration/position (dissociated sensory loss), matching this patient. MRI would show a syrinx within the cervical spinal cord.

Spinal cord metastasis (choice E) can occur where tumor can spread via the vasculature to, more commonly, the vertebral body and epidural space and can cause cord compression, sensory and motor dysfunction. Sources of metastasis include lungs, breast, and GI tract. Patients present with bone or radicular pain and/or motor or sensory deficits, but not specifically decreased pain and temperature sensation as seen in our patient.

stem: A 75-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of nausea, vomiting, and obtundation. She has a history of congestive heart failure, managed with diuretics. Laboratory studies show: Sodium 116 mEq/L, Potassium 4.1 mEq/L, BUN 15 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, Glucose 105 mg/dL. Her electrolyte imbalances are corrected via IV administration of electrolyte-containing fluids. Three days after the initiation of therapy the patient begins to show dysarthria, dysphagia, spastic quadriplegia, and confusion. This patient most likely has damage in which of the following neurologic structures?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Hyponatremia can result from conditions such as congestive heart failure, liver failure, kidney failure, and diuretics when electrolytes are not adequately monitored. Central pontine myelinolysis (also called osmotic demyelination syndrome, ODS) is a specific, and nearly always iatrogenic, condition characterized by demyelination of the central pons following overly rapid correction of severe hyponatremia (generally 120 mEq/L or less). Axons and neuronal cell bodies are relatively preserved. The lesion usually specifically involves the basis pontis and portions of the pontine tegmentum. Clinically, patients may develop a rapidly evolving spastic para- or quadriparesis, often accompanied by pseudobulbar symptoms such as dysarthria or dysphagia 2 to 6 days after aggressive IV fluid therapy with hypertonic saline solutions. Delirium and coma can also occur. Severely affected patients can develop "Locked-in" syndrome, in which they are awake, but unable to move or communicate except by vertical eye movements and blinking. The specific mechanism by which the pons is damaged is unclear. Conditions that predispose patients to this condition include alcoholism, liver disease, malnutrition, and hyponatremia. Approximately 10% of patients with this disorder can develop demyelination in extrapontine regions. However, the cerebellum (choice A), the cortex (choice B), the spinal cord (choice D), and the thalamus (choice E) are not specific targets in this condition.

The cerebellum (choice A), the cortex (choice B), the spinal cord (choice D), and the thalamus (choice E) are not specific targets in central pontine myelinolysis; the demyelination specifically involves the basis pontis and portions of the pontine tegmentum.

stem: A 7-year-old child is brought to the physician because of nausea, vomiting, and difficulty walking. His temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a wide-based, ataxic gait. CT scan of the head shows a mass in the cerebellar vermis. Microscopic examination of a biopsy specimen shows evidence of both neuronal and glial differentiation and occasional rosette formation. Which of the following is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
The correct answer is C. Medulloblastoma is the only tumor on the list characterized by both neuronal and glial differentiation. It is a primitive neuroectodermal tumor that is highly undifferentiated and originates from a primordial neuroglial precursor. It is predominantly a pediatric tumor; 75% occur in children. Medulloblastomas arise in the cerebellar vermis (infra-tentorial location), which accounts for this patient's truncal ataxia. Adult medulloblastomas are not common and more likely to be located in the lateral cerebellar hemispheres and less commonly in the cerebrum. Histologically, the tumor forms sheets of densely packed, poorly differentiated small cells. Occasional cells show spindle cell morphology and may stain for the glial marker glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Other occasional cells show neuronal differentiation and form rosettes. The tumor has a 50% 10-year survival rate when treated with combined surgery and radiation.

Ependymomas (choice A), in this age group, commonly arise from the fourth ventricle in the cerebellar region (infra-tentorial location); not the cerebellar vermis. These present as papillary masses, characteristically with perivascular rosettes. They can produce hydrocephalus by obstructing the flow of CSF.

Glioblastoma multiforme (choice B) and oligodendroglioma (choice E) are pure glial tumors occurring in adults and have a supratentorial (cortical) location. Glioblastoma multiforme is a high-grade astrocytoma associated with considerable necrosis and hemorrhage and has a poor prognosis. Oligodendrogliomas can have cytoplasmic clearing ("fried egg" appearance) with thin capillaries ("chicken wire" appearance).

Medulloblastoma is a primitive neuroectodermal tumor of childhood that arises in the cerebellar vermis and shows both neuronal and glial differentiation with rosette formation, matching this patient's ataxia and biopsy.

Meningioma (choice D) is a benign tumor of the meninges, most commonly the dura mater. It is usually slow-growing, most commonly occurring in the para-sagittal region, and compresses, but does not infiltrate, the underlying brain tissue. Women are more commonly affected and the tumor can have progesterone receptors. Psammoma bodies may be present, and the tumor may be part of a syndrome such as neurofibromatosis (NF1).

Glioblastoma multiforme is a high-grade astrocytoma associated with considerable necrosis and hemorrhage and has a poor prognosis. Oligodendrogliomas can have cytoplasmic clearing ("fried egg" appearance) with thin capillaries ("chicken wire" appearance).
